course.title: MSSP: SOC 2 + ISO 27001 Engagement
course.audience: Run a real client engagement — SOC 2 + ISO 27001 compliance as an MSSP analyst.
course.description: A full client engagement: scope the work, assess the gaps, implement and test controls, then assemble the audit evidence package. Three roles, mapped to SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001.

roles.name: Offensive Security (Penetration Tester)
roles.mission: Penetration testing and control validation for the client.

roles.name: Detection & Response (MDR Analyst)
roles.mission: Hardening, detection engineering and incident response for the client.

roles.name: Governance & Audit (vCISO)
roles.mission: Scope, risk, controls and the audit evidence spine.

gates.title: Scope & SoA signed
gates.description: The engagement agreement is signed and the Statement of Applicability defines which controls are in scope. Nothing is implemented before this.

gates.title: Controls implemented
gates.description: Every applicable control is implemented and mapped in the Control Matrix with an owner and its evidence source.

tasks.title: Kick-off & scope the engagement
tasks.objective: Sign the engagement paperwork and define exactly what the SOC 2 / ISO 27001 attestation covers.
learn: SOC 2 system description vs ISO 27001 Clause 4 scope
definitionOfDone: MSA/SOW/NDA recorded
System / ISMS boundary written
Sign-off captured

handoff.note: Red tests only what is in scope.
Blue instruments only in-scope systems.

steps.title: Record the engagement agreement
steps.description: Capture the client, engagement type, and terms.
steps.instruction: Fill the Engagement Agreement & Scope form: client, engagement type (SOC 2 / ISO / combined), NDA, and sign-off.
steps.whatItMeans: This is the contractual and ethical anchor — like the Scope & RoE in a pentest, nothing proceeds until it is signed.

steps.title: Define the system / ISMS boundary
steps.description: Draw the exact boundary the attestation covers.
steps.instruction: In the same form, write the in-scope systems, data and locations, plus what is explicitly out of scope.
steps.whatItMeans: The boundary determines which controls apply, what Red may test, and what evidence the auditor samples. Too wide wastes effort; too narrow fails the audit.

tasks.title: Confirm rules of engagement
tasks.objective: Agree the testing targets, windows, and written authorization before any scanning.
prerequisites: GRC has recorded the engagement scope
definitionOfDone: Targets + windows confirmed against scope
Authorization in writing

steps.title: Confirm targets and authorization
steps.description: Cross-check the in-scope hosts and get written testing authorization.
steps.instruction: Read GRC’s engagement scope; confirm the exact hosts/URLs, allowed test windows, and that you have written authorization to test them.
steps.whatItMeans: Testing outside the authorized scope is illegal and voids the engagement — the PTES pre-engagement step exists to prevent exactly that.

tasks.title: Stand up logging & sensors
tasks.objective: Centralize logs and baseline “normal” so later detections and evidence have data to work with.
prerequisites: GRC has defined the system boundary
definitionOfDone: Logs centralized for in-scope systems
A baseline of normal activity captured

steps.title: Enable and centralize auditing
steps.description: Turn on host auditing and confirm logs flow.
steps.command: sudo systemctl enable --now auditd && sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -ts today
steps.expectedOutput:
$ sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -ts today
----
time->Mon Aug  5 09:12:44 2026
type=USER_LOGIN msg=audit(1754384: pid=1442 uid=0 auid=1000
 msg='op=login id=1000 exe="/usr/sbin/sshd" hostname=10.10.100.5
 res=success'

outputHighlights.label: a real audit record. Its presence proves auditd is not just running but actually recording — an active service with no events is a silent gap.
the outcome field. Auditing both success and failure is what SOC 2 CC7 and ISO A.8.15 expect — a failed-login record would read res=failed here.
what caused the event. Tying an event to the program behind it is the difference between a log and evidence an auditor will accept.

steps.whatItMeans: Central, tamper-evident logging is the foundation of SOC 2 CC7 monitoring and ISO A.8.15 — you cannot detect or evidence what you do not log.
steps.troubleshooting: No output → auditd may not be installed: `sudo apt install auditd`. On a container, use journald: `journalctl -u ssh --since today`.

tasks.title: Risk assessment & Statement of Applicability
tasks.objective: Assess the client against the frameworks and decide which controls apply (the SoA).
prerequisites: Engagement scope signed (Gate 1 depends on this)
definitionOfDone: ≥3 Annex A controls with applicability decisions
Every applicable control justified

handoff.note: Blue implements the technical controls the SoA marks applicable.

steps.title: Assess risk and decide applicability
steps.description: For each Annex A control, decide whether it applies and why.
steps.instruction: Fill the Statement of Applicability form: add each Annex A control in scope, its applicability (Yes/No), the justification, and its status.
steps.whatItMeans: The SoA is the ISO 27001 centrepiece — the auditor reads it first to see what you claim and why. It also feeds the SOC 2 control set.

steps.title: Export the SoA and hash it
steps.description: The export, fingerprinted before anyone edits it.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the exported SoA and appends the line to the evidence hash list the packet will cite.

steps.whatItMeans: An auditor samples the SoA as it stood when the controls were chosen. The hash is how you prove this is that version.

steps.title: Count the applicable controls
steps.description: How many controls apply, from the file, not from memory.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Counts the rows marked applicable. The number goes in the SoA summary and must match the matrix next week.

steps.whatItMeans: The SoA says how big the control set is. Counting it from the export catches the row someone marked twice.

tasks.title: External attack-surface assessment
tasks.objective: Map the in-scope external attack surface to feed the gap analysis.
prerequisites: Rules of engagement confirmed
definitionOfDone: In-scope hosts port-scanned
TLS/exposure issues noted for the gap analysis

handoff.note: GRC folds exposure gaps into the risk assessment.

steps.title: Scan the in-scope hosts
steps.description: Enumerate services on the authorized targets.

commands.explain: Service/version scan of one authorized host.

steps.expectedOutput:
Nmap scan report for 10.10.100.30
Host is up (0.00051s latency).

PORT    STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.7
443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx 1.14.0 (Ubuntu)
3389/tcp open ms-wbt-server Microsoft Terminal Services

Service detection performed. Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up)

outputHighlights.label: an old SSH version. In a gap assessment the exact version is the finding — it maps to specific advisories the client must patch.
RDP exposed to the network. Remote Desktop reachable externally is a classic high-risk gap that goes straight into the risk assessment.
you scanned exactly the one authorised host. Anything more would be outside the agreed scope and window.

steps.whatItMeans: A repeatable, authorized scan (NIST 800-115) is the credible basis for the “technical vulnerability” side of the gap assessment.
steps.troubleshooting: “Host seems down” → keep `-Pn`. No permission/blocked → confirm the host is in the authorized scope and window.

tasks.title: CIS baseline gap scan
tasks.objective: Measure current hardening against the CIS Benchmarks to find the control gaps.
prerequisites: Log centralization from Week 0 done
SSH / console access to the in-scope hosts
The relevant CIS Benchmark PDF to score against
definitionOfDone: Baseline scan run
Top hardening gaps recorded for Week 2

handoff.note: GRC references gaps when building the control matrix.

steps.title: Run a hardening audit
steps.description: Scan the host against a CIS-style baseline.
steps.expectedOutput:
[+] Results
  Warnings (1):
  ! SSH root login is permitted [SSH-7412]
  Suggestions (14):
  * Set a password on GRUB bootloader [BOOT-5122]
  * Disable core dumps for setuid programs [KRNL-5820]

  Hardening index : 58 [###########         ]

outputHighlights.label: the baseline score. Its whole value is the before/after pair — record it now so Week 2’s fixes have something to be measured against.
a warning, and warnings are your priority gaps. This one maps directly to SOC 2 CC6 access controls.
the test ID. Quoting it makes the gap traceable in the control matrix — an auditor can look up exactly what was checked.

steps.whatItMeans: Gaps against CIS map directly to SOC 2 CC6 and ISO A.8 controls, turning “harden the box” into auditable control work.
steps.troubleshooting: `lynis: command not found` → `sudo apt install lynis` (or run from a cloned copy).

tasks.title: Build the control matrix
tasks.objective: Map every control to its SOC 2 CC and ISO Annex A references, assign an owner, and name the evidence.
prerequisites: SoA complete (Gate 1)
definitionOfDone: ≥3 controls with SOC 2 or ISO references
Every control has an owner + evidence source

handoff.note: Blue implements and evidences the controls it owns.

steps.title: Map controls and assign owners
steps.description: Create the working crosswalk of controls.
steps.instruction: Fill the Control Matrix form: one row per control with its SOC 2 CC, ISO Annex A, owner, status, and the evidence an auditor would sample.
steps.whatItMeans: Build the control once and satisfy both frameworks — the matrix is how a multi-framework MSSP avoids doing the work twice.

steps.title: Export the matrix and hash it
steps.description: The crosswalk, fingerprinted.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the control matrix and records it for the evidence packet.

steps.whatItMeans: The matrix is the artefact both frameworks are audited against; a dated hash is what makes a later change visible.

steps.title: Check every control has an owner
steps.description: No row without an owner survives the export.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Counts matrix rows whose owner column is empty. Zero is the only acceptable answer before the hand-off.

steps.whatItMeans: A control nobody owns is a control nobody operates. The count is the check the auditor would otherwise make for you.

tasks.title: Implement the technical controls
tasks.objective: Stand up the missing controls GRC assigned and record what changed.
prerequisites: Control Matrix assigns Blue’s controls
definitionOfDone: Assigned controls implemented
Each change recorded for the evidence trail

handoff.note: GRC updates the matrix status to Implemented/Operating with evidence.

steps.title: Enforce baseline access controls
steps.description: Apply a default-deny firewall and log the change.

commands.explain: Block all inbound by default.
Permit only the services you intend to expose.
Turn the firewall on.

steps.expectedOutput:
$ sudo ufw status verbose
Status: active
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), disabled (routed)

To         Action      From
--         ------      ----
22/tcp     ALLOW IN    Anywhere

outputHighlights.label: the control is actually enforcing. An "inactive" firewall with correct rules is a control that exists on paper but not in operation — the exact thing an auditor tests for.
the default-deny posture CC6.6 and ISO A.8.20 expect. Everything is blocked unless explicitly allowed below.
the one justified exception. A short, reasoned allow-list is the evidence — a long one undermines the default-deny claim.

steps.whatItMeans: This is a control implementation, not just a config — record it so it becomes sampled evidence in the matrix and packet.
steps.troubleshooting: Locked out of SSH? Always `ufw allow 22/tcp` BEFORE enabling. On a remote box, keep an open session while you test.

tasks.title: Threat-model the proposed controls
tasks.objective: Check the controls being implemented against the attack paths found in Week 1, and say which ones actually close them.
prerequisites: Attack-surface findings from Week 1
Control Matrix with owners assigned (in progress)
learn: Threat modelling against a control set
definitionOfDone: Every Week-1 finding mapped to the control that is meant to close it
Any finding with no control covering it raised to GRC before the gate

handoff.note: GRC records the uncovered findings in the matrix as gaps or accepted risks, with a reason.
Blue implements the controls that close a real finding first.

steps.title: Map each finding to the control that closes it
steps.description: Walk the Week-1 findings against the control matrix.
steps.instruction: Walk your Week-1 findings against the control matrix.
instructionList: For each finding, name the control in the matrix meant to close it.
Say how you would retest that finding once the control is in.
Where no control closes a finding, write it down and tell GRC.
steps.whatItMeans: An auditor asks whether a control addresses the risk it claims to. Checking that while the controls are still being built beats finding out in Week 4 that one closes nothing.

steps.title: Export the threat model rows and hash them
steps.description: The finding-to-control map, fingerprinted.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the gap assessment that now carries the control mapping, so the Week 4 retest compares against this version.

steps.whatItMeans: The retest is judged against the findings as they stood here. The hash fixes what “here” means.

steps.title: Check every finding names a control
steps.description: No finding without the control that closes it.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Counts findings, then counts control references. The second number must be at least the first.

steps.whatItMeans: A finding mapped to no control is risk nobody has decided to own. The two counts make that visible in one line.

tasks.title: Penetration test & retest
tasks.objective: Test the implemented controls, then retest every fix to prove closure.
prerequisites: Controls implemented (Gate 2)
definitionOfDone: Findings tested
Every high/critical retested and recorded Closed/Open/Risk-accepted

handoff.note: Blue uses the attack timeline to validate detections.

steps.title: Test and record findings
steps.description: Run the authorized test against the in-scope app.
steps.instruction: Perform the authorized test; for each finding, record severity, remediation, and (after the fix) the retest result in the form.
steps.whatItMeans: A finding that is fixed and retested Closed is the strongest operating-effectiveness evidence for CC4.1 / A.8.8 — “we test, and the fixes hold”.

steps.title: Re-run the scan against the hardened host
steps.description: The retest scan, same flags, saved to a file.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: The same scan as Week 1, saved. The count of open ports is the before/after number the retest report leads with.
commands.sample:
Nmap scan report for <target_ip>
22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH 9.6p1
443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx 1.24.0
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up)
2

steps.expectedOutput:
Nmap scan report for <target_ip>
22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH 9.6p1
443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx 1.24.0
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up)
2
steps.whatItMeans: A retest that re-runs the original scan is the only honest comparison. Fewer open ports is the finding closing in front of you.

steps.title: Hash the retest evidence
steps.description: The scan and the proof files, fingerprinted.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the retest scan and the report, so the attestation in Week 4 cites files that cannot change.

steps.whatItMeans: The tester’s attestation is worth what its evidence is worth. Hashed scan output is evidence; a screenshot is a claim.

tasks.title: Detection engineering
tasks.objective: Write detections mapped to ATT&CK and validate them against the Red team’s activity.
prerequisites: Red is running the test (attack telemetry available)
definitionOfDone: ≥2 detections mapped to ATT&CK
≥1 validated as Fired against Red’s test

handoff.note: GRC references validated detections as CC7 evidence.

steps.title: Write and validate detections
steps.description: Author detections for the attacks Red is running.
steps.instruction: For each attack technique, add a detection to the Detection Rules form — log source, ATT&CK id, logic — then mark whether it fired during Red’s test.
steps.whatItMeans: Detections that provably catch a real attack satisfy SOC 2 CC7.2/7.3 monitoring — not “we have a SIEM” but “our monitoring works”.

steps.title: Spot the attack in the logs
steps.description: Confirm the attack is visible in your log source.

outputHighlights.label: a classic injection probe in a URL. Real users never send this — a match is what proves your detection has genuine attack data to fire on, not a hypothetical.
the attacker’s IP during the test window. Record it and the timestamp — these become the metrics that show the detection actually caught Red’s activity.
a second, different technique. Two distinct payloads landing lets you map more than one ATT&CK id to real evidence.

steps.whatItMeans: Seeing the attack in the logs is the difference between a theoretical rule and a validated detection.
steps.troubleshooting: No matches → check the correct log path (`/var/log/nginx/access.log`) and that the test actually hit this host.

tasks.title: Coordinate validation & collect evidence
tasks.objective: Track remediation to closure and start collecting the evidence each control needs.
prerequisites: Retest results from Red (what closed, what remains)
Control Matrix with an owner and evidence named per control (Gate 2)
definitionOfDone: Findings tracked to closure
Evidence gathered for each implemented control

steps.title: Track remediation and gather evidence
steps.description: Update control status and collect the sampled artifacts.
steps.instruction: For each control in the matrix, move status toward Operating and collect the concrete evidence artifact (config, log, ticket, report).
steps.whatItMeans: Auditors sample evidence, not intentions — collecting it as you go turns Week 4 from a scramble into an assembly job.

steps.title: Hash the evidence collected this week
steps.description: Every file in the packet folder, fingerprinted.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: One hash per collected file. The packet cites these lines, so collect first, hash second, never edit after.

steps.whatItMeans: Chain of custody for an audit is a list of hashes with dates. This file is that list.

steps.title: Verify the hashes still match
steps.description: The check an auditor runs on day one.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Re-hashes every file and compares. OK on every line, or the evidence has changed since collection.

steps.whatItMeans: Collecting evidence is half the job; proving it is unchanged is the other half. This line is the proof.

handoff.note: Your section of the Retest & Remediation-Validation Report, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Close out the retest and attest
tasks.objective: Finish the Retest & Validation report — every finding resolved one way or another — and attest to the result for the evidence packet.
prerequisites: Week-3 findings recorded with remediations
Fixes deployed by Blue
learn: Risk acceptance with a named owner
definitionOfDone: Every finding reads Closed, Open or Risk accepted — none left blank
The methodology section states how each retest was performed
Anything still Open or Risk accepted names who accepted it and why

handoff.note: GRC files it in the evidence packet as the operating-effectiveness evidence for CC4.1 / A.8.8.

steps.title: Resolve every finding and attest
steps.description: Retest what is still open, then attest to the result.
steps.instruction: Take the report from “tested” to “closed out”.
instructionList: Retest anything still open from Week 3 and set its result.
For each Open or Risk-accepted finding, record who accepted it and why.
Fill the methodology section: how the retests were done, not just that they were.
steps.whatItMeans: The auditor’s question is not “did you test?” but “what happened to what you found?”. A blank retest column is an open finding by default, and a risk accepted without a named owner is an omission, not an acceptance.

steps.title: Verify the retest evidence hashes
steps.description: Every line OK before the attestation is signed.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Re-hashes every file the report cites and compares. The attestation is signed only when every line reads OK.

steps.whatItMeans: Signing an attestation over evidence you have not re-verified is how testers lose their names. One command removes the risk.

steps.title: Record the accepted risks
steps.description: The findings the client chose not to fix, counted and dated.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Counts the accepted-risk rows and stamps today. Both go into the attestation as written.

steps.whatItMeans: A risk the client accepts is still a risk; the retest records who accepted it and when, so nobody later calls it an oversight.

tasks.title: Report detection & response metrics
tasks.objective: Compute the MTTD/MTTR and coverage numbers a Type II auditor samples for CC7.
prerequisites: Detections deployed and validated against Red’s activity (Week 3)
Alert/incident timestamps available to compute MTTD/MTTR
definitionOfDone: MTTD and MTTR recorded
Coverage + window set

steps.title: Report the response metrics
steps.description: Summarize detection/response performance over the window.
steps.instruction: Fill the Detection & Response Metrics form from your SIEM/IR tickets: incidents, MTTD, MTTR, coverage, false-positive rate.
steps.whatItMeans: Numbers over an observation window are what turns a Type I “designed” control into Type II “operating effectively”.

steps.title: Count the detections and the responses in the log
steps.description: Fired, triaged, closed: three numbers from the SIEM export.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.cmd: grep -c "alert" siem-export.json && grep -c "\"status\": \"closed\"" siem-export.json && echo "METRICS counted"
commands.explain: Alerts raised, then alerts closed, from the exported month. The ratio is the detection-and-response metric the report leads with.

steps.whatItMeans: A metric typed from memory is an opinion; one counted from the export is a measurement. The report wants the second kind.

steps.title: Hash the metrics export
steps.description: The month’s export, fingerprinted for the packet.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the export and the report so CC7 evidence in the packet is the file the numbers came from.

steps.whatItMeans: CC7.2 asks whether you monitor and respond. The hashed export is the answer an auditor can re-derive.

handoff.note: Your section of the Detection & Response Metrics, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Run the internal audit
tasks.objective: Do the mandatory ISO 9.2 internal audit before the external auditor arrives.
prerequisites: Control Matrix + evidence collected
definitionOfDone: Findings recorded with results
Every nonconformity has a corrective action

handoff.note: Fix nonconformities before assembling the packet.

steps.title: Audit your own controls
steps.description: Independently review each control against its evidence.
steps.instruction: Fill the Internal Audit Report form: for each control, record conformity / minor NC / major NC and a corrective action with an owner.
steps.whatItMeans: Finding and fixing your own nonconformities first is the whole point of the internal audit — it is far cheaper than the external auditor finding them.

steps.title: Export the audit report and hash it
steps.description: The report, fingerprinted at sign-off.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Fingerprints the signed audit report for the packet.

steps.whatItMeans: Clause 9.2 wants the audit result as a record. A hashed export is a record that cannot be quietly improved later.

steps.title: Count the nonconformities
steps.description: Minor and major, from the export.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: Counts the findings the corrective-action plan has to carry. Each one needs an owner and a date.

steps.whatItMeans: Clause 10.2 turns each nonconformity into a corrective action. Counting them is how you know the plan is complete.

tasks.title: Assemble the audit evidence packet
tasks.objective: Index every control to its evidence artifact so the external auditor can sample it.
prerequisites: Internal audit complete
All role deliverables in
definitionOfDone: ≥3 evidence items tied to controls
Every item has an owner + location
Team package exported

steps.title: Index the evidence to controls
steps.description: Build the auditor’s index of evidence.
steps.instruction: Fill the Audit Evidence Packet form: one row per evidence artifact, tied to its SOC 2 CC / ISO Annex A control, with owner, type, location and period.
steps.whatItMeans: A control mapped to concrete evidence is a control an auditor can pass. This packet is the deliverable that gets the client through Type I / Stage 1.

steps.title: Export the engagement package
steps.description: Produce the final submission bundle.
steps.instruction: On the Deliverables page, click Download team package to produce the zip of all eight engagement deliverables.
steps.whatItMeans: One clean package — agreement, SoA, control matrix, validation, detections, metrics, internal audit, evidence — is what you hand the auditor.

steps.title: Hash the finished packet
steps.description: The index and every file it names.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.explain: The packet index and every cited file, fingerprinted together. This is the list the auditor receives.

steps.whatItMeans: The packet is only as good as the proof that nothing in it moved. One hash list, handed over with it.

steps.title: Confirm every index row points at a real file
steps.description: No citation to a file that does not exist.
steps.instruction: Run it in the team evidence folder and paste the output.

commands.cmd: awk -F, 'NR>1 {print $3}' 08_Audit_Evidence_Packet.csv | while read f; do [ -f "$f" ] && echo "FOUND $f" || echo "MISSING $f"; done
commands.explain: Walks the packet’s file column and says FOUND or MISSING per row. A MISSING line is a citation the auditor cannot follow.

steps.whatItMeans: An evidence packet with a broken reference fails the audit on a technicality. The loop finds it before the auditor does.

steps.title: Write the Portfolio
steps.description: The repository, the case study, three resume bullets, the diagram and the skills shown, on the shared Portfolio form.
steps.instruction: Fill the Portfolio with the whole team.
instructionList: Paste the link to the team repository, e.g. https://github.com/org/capstone-team01, that holds the configuration and documents.
Write the case study in two hundred words or more: the problem, what was built, the decisions, the result.
Write three resume bullets, each an action, a tool and a measurable result, e.g. "closed 14 of 15 findings".
Name the diagram the case study refers to, then list the skills demonstrated with the evidence for each.
steps.expectedOutput: The Portfolio is filled: a repository link, a case study of two hundred words or more, three bullets, the diagram named, three or more skills with evidence.

docs.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010: architecture description
docs.lookFor: What an architecture description must identify: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the rationale for decisions.

steps.whatItMeans: The certification proves what was learned; the Portfolio proves what was built. An employer reads this form, not the pass mark.

fixes.symptom: The case-study check stays red at two hundred words
fixes.fix: Words are counted on whitespace; a line of bullet dashes or a table is one word each. Write sentences.

fixes.symptom: The repository link is refused
fixes.fix: It has to start with https:// and hold no spaces; paste the address bar, not the repository name.

handoff.note: Your section of the Audit Evidence Packet, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: AI extension: map a control to evidence
tasks.objective: Use a local AI assistant on what you built this week: map a control to evidence, grounded and checked.

steps.title: Run a local model
steps.description: A model that runs on your own machine, offline.
steps.instruction: Pull a small local model and list it.

DOMAINS.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the commands the job needs?
DOMAINS.evidence: A verification record per step: the output hash, the tokens matched, the attempts, and a receipt in cloud mode.

DOMAINS.label: Professional execution
DOMAINS.definition: Procedures followed to standard, steps in order, first pastes, evidence named, checks met, documents controlled, work on time.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and deliver on the calendar?
DOMAINS.evidence: The order of verification stamps, the attempts, the file names, the Definition-of-Done checks, the control block and the cohort due dates.

DOMAINS.label: Problem solving
DOMAINS.definition: Faults logged and resolved, steps verified after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes from first paste to proof.
DOMAINS.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?
DOMAINS.evidence: Fault, incident and triage rows with their outcome column, retries that verified, the append-only flag history and two stamps per step.

DOMAINS.label: Thought process
DOMAINS.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options with rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback, and reasons written on change rows.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?
DOMAINS.evidence: Decision blocks with the option chosen, who chose it and when, the answers to the supporting questions, and the form lifecycle.

DOMAINS.label: Architecture and design
DOMAINS.definition: Design briefs, topologies, IP plans, bills of materials, decision records and as-built documents drafted, approved and issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member design a system and write it down so another team can build it?
DOMAINS.evidence: The architecture and configuration forms of the role: rows filled, checks met, approved or issued, with the decisions on them.

DOMAINS.label: Team and communication
DOMAINS.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given, steps ticked for teammates, reports filed, notes written, handovers issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPIS.label: Values recalled
KPIS.numerator: Recall activities answered correctly: the value the team recorded, picked among distractors.
KPIS.denominator: Recall activities answered, from the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Weeks after recording an address, a prefix, a port or a decision, the member still knows it.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention of the project the member built, read from answers given without the form open.

KPIS.label: Scenarios applied
KPIS.numerator: Applied scenarios answered correctly: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size.
KPIS.denominator: Applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Takes a value the team recorded and uses it under a change the course did not script.
KPIS.whyCompany: Applied use of recorded facts, not recall alone; offered scenarios count whether or not answered.

KPIS.label: Conflicts resolved
KPIS.numerator: Conflicts the record found that the team resolved: the address, the port, the prefix, the size no longer at odds.
KPIS.denominator: Conflicts the record found at the checkpoints reached, resolved or still open.
KPIS.whyMember: A duplicate address or an over-committed host found by the platform and fixed by the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Contradictions in the record closed, read from the record itself rather than from a claim.

KPIS.label: Minutes on task
KPIS.numerator: Whole minutes the member had tasks of this course open on a visible tab, pauses excluded.
KPIS.denominator: A count; nothing is read into it.
KPIS.whyMember: How long the work took the member, by the timer they can pause; measured, never rewarded.
KPIS.whyCompany: Time on task as context for the other rows; no score reads it.

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Technical capability
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: What the member can do: skills, commands and procedures proven by output against the exam and the role.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the procedures the job needs?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Problem solving
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Faults logged and resolved, verifications reached after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes between first paste and proof.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professional execution
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: How the work was done: steps in order, first pastes, evidence named to convention, every check due met.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and leave evidence an auditor can find?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Decision making
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options, justified, approved by the team, and changes with a rollback written.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Teamwork
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given and steps ticked on teammates’ tasks.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly and hold their lane in a team?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professionalism
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, documents controlled, controls cited, instructor approval earned.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member deliver on time, to standard, and to the reviewer’s satisfaction?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Growth
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Skills proved twice, retained across weeks, verified faster week on week, and the gap to a work role closing.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Understanding
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Values the team recorded, recalled and applied weeks later; conflicts the record found, resolved; minutes on task, measured.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Did this member retain what the team built, and can they apply it when something changes?

METRICS.note: R140: the activity asks for a value the team recorded; the distractors come from the record.

METRICS.label: Scenarios applied
METRICS.definition: Applied scenarios answered correctly, over applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
METRICS.note: R140: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size doubled.

METRICS.label: Conflicts resolved
METRICS.definition: Conflicts the record found that are no longer present, over conflicts found, once the apply checkpoint is reached.
METRICS.note: R140: read from the record itself; the answer only says the team looked.

METRICS.label: Minutes on task
METRICS.definition: Whole minutes the member had tasks open on a visible tab, pauses and hidden tabs excluded; a count.
METRICS.note: R140: the timer the member can pause; measured, never rewarded.

PRACTICES.label: Default deny
PRACTICES.definition: Nothing passes a boundary unless a rule allows it; the allow list is the policy.

PRACTICES.label: Encryption in transit
PRACTICES.definition: Traffic crosses a boundary only over approved TLS versions, and the weak ones are refused.

PRACTICES.label: Hash evidence at capture
PRACTICES.definition: Every artifact is hashed when it is saved and the digest is recorded, so later copies can be checked.

PRACTICES.label: Authorised testing only
PRACTICES.definition: Scanning and attacks happen inside a signed scope and rules of engagement, against the pod the team owns.

PRACTICES.label: Agreed scope and terms
PRACTICES.definition: The work starts from a written agreement: what is in scope, what is out, and who signs.

PRACTICES.label: Retest to closure
PRACTICES.definition: A finding is closed only by a retest that shows the fix, and every finding ends Closed, Open or Risk accepted.

PRACTICES.label: Likelihood-times-impact scoring
PRACTICES.definition: Each risk is scored on a stated scale for likelihood and impact, and the score decides the order.

PRACTICES.label: Threat modelling
PRACTICES.definition: Threats are enumerated per component with a method, and each is tied to a control or an accepted risk.

PRACTICES.label: Compensating controls
PRACTICES.definition: Where a control cannot be applied, another control covering the same risk is named and justified.

PRACTICES.label: Change control
PRACTICES.definition: Every change is requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded before it reaches a system.

PRACTICES.label: Hardening baseline
PRACTICES.definition: Hosts are configured to a written benchmark and checked against it, so drift from the baseline is visible.

PRACTICES.label: Configuration scanning
PRACTICES.definition: Hosts are scanned against a benchmark on a schedule, and the failed checks become findings.

PRACTICES.label: Guardrail regression tests
PRACTICES.definition: Every blocked attack case becomes a test the pipeline runs, so a removed guardrail fails the build.

PRACTICES.label: Detection as code
PRACTICES.definition: Detections are written as versioned rules, mapped to a technique id and validated against a test attack.

PRACTICES.label: ATT&CK-mapped reporting
PRACTICES.definition: Findings, indicators and detections carry the technique id, so they can be compared across teams.

PRACTICES.label: Sign and version documents
PRACTICES.definition: A document carries an id, a version, an owner, a date and a status, and a change makes a new version.

PRACTICES.label: Control mapping
PRACTICES.definition: Each control is mapped to the criteria it satisfies across frameworks, with an owner and an evidence source.

PRACTICES.label: Evidence by design
PRACTICES.definition: Every control names the evidence that proves it operates, and the evidence is collected as the work happens.

PRACTICES.label: Corrective action
PRACTICES.definition: Every nonconformity gets a cause, a corrective action, an owner and a date, and the action is checked.

PRACTICES.label: Metrics with targets
PRACTICES.definition: Each metric has a formula, a source and a target, so a number can be read as good or bad.

PRACTICES.label: Customer assurance
PRACTICES.definition: A customer question is answered with evidence or an honest gap, never with a promise.

PRACTICES.label: Input and output guardrails
PRACTICES.definition: Prompts and model outputs pass through filters that block or contain the listed attack cases.

PRACTICES.label: Human checkpoint
PRACTICES.definition: AI-assisted work passes a named human check before it is acted on, and the check is recorded.

PRACTICES.label: Suites with a pass line
PRACTICES.definition: An attack or evaluation suite states what passing means before it runs.

SCORING.label: Tool proficiency
SCORING.definition: Commands and skills proven by output, and skills proved on a second task, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Reads browser checks and receipts of stamps, not proof of the machine; the per-tool table names each command.

SCORING.label: Troubleshooting success
SCORING.definition: Faults resolved, retries that verified, stuck flags cleared and steps resolved within the hour, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Faults are team rows; the minutes are a median between two recorded stamps, so a step left open overnight is counted apart.

SCORING.label: Judgment
SCORING.definition: Decisions recorded, justified and approved, and changes with a rollback written, equally weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Counts what was written against named options; it does not judge whether the choice was right.

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SCORING.label: Understanding retained
SCORING.definition: Values recalled, scenarios applied and conflicts resolved, weeks after the team recorded them, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Asks only about values the team recorded; before the checkpoint week the score stands on nothing and says so.

SOPS.label: Change record
SOPS.definition: A change written before it is made: what, where, the backup, the approval, the rollback and the result.

SOPS.label: Scope and rules of engagement
SOPS.definition: What may be tested, when, how, by whom, and the signatures that authorise it.

SOPS.label: Hardening baseline
SOPS.definition: The settings a host must have, the benchmark they come from, and the proof each host meets them.

SOPS.label: Risk register
SOPS.definition: Each risk with its likelihood, impact, score, owner and treatment, reviewed on a schedule.

SOPS.label: Monitoring plan
SOPS.definition: What is watched, from which sources, who is alerted, and what a page means.

SOPS.label: Detection rules
SOPS.definition: Detections as versioned rules with the technique id and the test that proved each fires.

SOPS.label: Control mapping
SOPS.definition: Each control mapped to the criteria it meets, with an owner and the evidence that proves it.

SOPS.label: Governance report
SOPS.definition: What leadership must decide, the risks accepted, the metrics and the open items.

SOPS.label: Internal audit
SOPS.definition: A planned audit against the standard with findings, nonconformities and corrective actions.

SOPS.label: Audit evidence packet
SOPS.definition: The evidence an examiner samples, tied to controls, each item with an owner and a location.

SOPS.label: Assessment report
SOPS.definition: Findings with severity, evidence and a fix, from a test that was scoped and authorised.

SOPS.label: Retest and validation record
SOPS.definition: Every finding retested and closed, left open or risk-accepted with a named owner.

SOPS.label: Portfolio record
SOPS.definition: The repository, a case study, three resume bullets, the architecture diagram and the skills demonstrated, for one project.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: OWASP
STANDARDS.description: OWASP Top 10 and the Web Security Testing Guide
STANDARDS.why: Catalogues the most common web application weaknesses. This tag means the step attacks or defends one of those top risks, the shared language developers use to talk about web security.

STANDARDS.label: CVSS
STANDARDS.description: Common Vulnerability Scoring System
STANDARDS.why: A 0 to 10 severity score for vulnerabilities. It turns "this is bad" into a consistent number, so stakeholders can rank findings and decide what to fix first.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-115
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
STANDARDS.why: The standard method for security testing and assessment. Following it makes scanning and exploitation repeatable, authorised and credible in a report.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 information security management system
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: SOC 2
STANDARDS.description: AICPA Trust Services Criteria for a SOC 2 examination
STANDARDS.why: The AICPA attestation standard built on the Trust Services Criteria: Security is CC1 to CC9, plus Availability, Confidentiality and the rest. This tag means the step produces a control or the evidence a SOC 2 Type I or II examiner samples.

STANDARDS.label: STRIDE
STANDARDS.description: STRIDE threat modelling
STANDARDS.why: A threat modelling lens: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. It names the category of threat this step addresses.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: NIST AI RMF
STANDARDS.description: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and its Generative AI Profile
STANDARDS.why: The AI framework Ridgeline adopts: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. A tag here means the step produces something an AI risk register or the AI questions a buyer asks will ask for.

STANDARDS.label: OWASP LLM Top 10
STANDARDS.description: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
STANDARDS.why: The shared catalogue of LLM application weaknesses: prompt injection, sensitive disclosure, excessive agency and the rest. A tag here names the weakness the step attacks or defends.

STANDARDS.label: MITRE ATLAS
STANDARDS.description: MITRE ATLAS: adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems
STANDARDS.why: ATT&CK for AI: real-world techniques attackers use against models and their data. Mapping a case to an ATLAS technique makes it comparable with the threat intelligence everyone else holds.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-30
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-30 Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
STANDARDS.why: The federal method for a risk assessment: threat sources, events, likelihood and impact. A risk register that follows it can be defended line by line.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-218
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
STANDARDS.why: The practices a secure software pipeline follows: protect the code, produce well-secured software, respond to vulnerabilities. A pipeline record that cites it names the gate each practice became.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27005
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27005 information security risk management
STANDARDS.why: The risk method behind ISO 27001 clause 6: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat. A risk register that cites it reads the same way to an auditor.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 architecture description
STANDARDS.why: What an architecture description must contain: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the decisions behind them. A solution architecture document that cites it is complete rather than a diagram.

STANDARDS.label: PTES
STANDARDS.description: Penetration Testing Execution Standard
STANDARDS.why: The seven phases of a penetration test, from pre-engagement and intelligence gathering to reporting. A test that cites it can show it was scoped, authorised and complete.

STANDARDS.label: MITRE ATT&CK
STANDARDS.description: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise: adversary tactics and techniques
STANDARDS.why: The shared vocabulary for adversary behaviour: fourteen tactics and the techniques under them. A detection or an indicator mapped to a technique id is comparable with the work of every other team.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).
